title: Here's Another Way of Thinking About Schemas
author: Dynamic Learning
summary: A cognitive-science newsletter piece proposes a third way of thinking about schemas, beyond the familiar container model (schemas as storage bins for facts) and network model (schemas as linked nodes). Drawing on a 2026 paper by Gibson, Azukas, and Soylu that connects embodied cognition to cognitive load theory, the author reframes schemas as dynamical-system attractors -- stable patterns a mind's activity repeatedly settles into, much like a marble rolling to the bottom of a bowl regardless of where it starts. Under this model, learning isn't filling a container or forging links; it's reshaping an entire knowledge landscape so that useful patterns become more likely to emerge, and updating one schema can ripple into related ones. The piece also uses the model to explain retrieval as reconstruction rather than exact recall, following Bartlett, and to explain why some schemas become self-sealing and resist correction even against strong contrary evidence. The author is candid that the framework is speculative, but argues it usefully straightens out some of the conceptual confusion in how schemas are usually taught.
points: Proposes a third model of schemas beyond the container (fills with information) and network (links information) models: a dynamical-systems model where schemas are attractor states the mind repeatedly settles into.

The marble-in-a-bowl metaphor reframes updating a schema as reshaping the whole knowledge landscape, not just adding a fact to a fixed slot -- explaining why one correction can ripple into unrelated related knowledge.
Retrieval, on this model, is reconstruction rather than replay: the system retrieves the gist of a settled pattern, which can include errors, echoing Bartlett's classic account of memory.
Some schemas become self-sealing and resist correction even against strong contrary evidence, which the dynamical model explains as an unusually deep, hard-to-reshape valley.
quotes: Recently, Gibson, Azukas, and Soylu (2026) have perhaps inadvertently provided an alternative way of approaching schemas while offering valuable insights into the relationship between embodied cognition and cognitive load theory.

Gibson et al. use the example of a marble rolling around a bowl to explain this. No matter where you place the marble on the rim, it will eventually settle at the bottom. The bottom of the bowl represents an attractor, a state towards which dynamic systems naturally gravitate.
Schemas, therefore, aren't assembled - they emerge via interactions between perception, memory, action, language, and prior knowledge, gradually producing a stable pattern.
Sometimes, new information doesn't just change the existing valley, but alters the entire landscape, potentially changing relationships among lots of existing knowledge.
If schemas are emergent, self-organising patterns, then effective learning isn't simply about adding to long-term memory. It's about repeatedly challenging (or perturbing) a knowledge system

Sometimes new information fails to assimilate (telling someone opposed to vaccines that they are safe and necessary may not lead to change, no matter the weight of evidence). We can think of these schemas as self-sealing.
